content.title: Author response
content.comment:
We hope that we could resolve your concerns in the discussion period.

1. Novelty

The objective of adversarial robustness is to obtain a robust model against adversarial attacks. The procedure of adversarial training is to perform an adversarial attack on every iteration, so the model learns how the adversarial attack is performed to the model. However, in our case, the margin-based watermarking does not perform the same type of attack during training. We empirically prove that learning with margin to trigger set can modify the decision boundary and improve the robustness against functionality stealing attack. Moreover, the margin is only applied for the trigger set where the adversarial training utilizes the margin for every training instance. We believe that our method has some similar points with adversarial training but the main idea is clearly differentiable.

2. The experiments are conducted on the small datasets

For computer vision applications, the CIFAR10/100 and SVHN can be considered as small datasets for evaluation. However, we believe that watermarking deep neural networks do not show acceptable performance for CIFAR10/100 and SVHN. In addition, recent studies of watermarking show the performance for CIFAR10/100 and SVHN [1,2].

---
[1] Jia et al., Entangled Watermarks as a defense against model extraction, Usenix Security Symposium 2021.

[2] Bansal et al., Certified Neural Network Watermarks with Randomized Smoothing, ICML 2022.

content.title: Author response
content.comment:
We hope that we could resolve your concerns in the discussion period.

1. Evaluation of the ambiguity attack

First of all, our method is to defend against the black-box attack (especially, functionality stealing attacks) so we cannot directly perform an ambiguity attack on the watermarked model since the attack requires multiple times of gradient descent for constructing the perturbation. 
However, the ambiguity attack can be applied to the surrogate models from the functionality stealing attacks, so we provide the results of that scenario. We set the ambiguity attack by 1) selecting random 100 images from the validation set (which does not have any conflicts with our trigger set), 2) performing the adversarial attack to obtain the label of chosen images, 3) naming them as the new trigger set for the adversary. The result shows that with the adversarial perturbation, the new trigger set shows 100% accuracy for new trigger labels, which means that the stolen model cannot defend the ambiguity attack.
For defending against such ambiguity attack, the model should show the perfect adversarial robustness since if the adversarial example exists, then the adversary can choose them as the new trigger set. In recent works of adversarial robustness, none of the methods and models show perfect robustness. Obviously, there is no guarantee that the surrogate model from the functionality stealing attack is perfectly robust against adversarial attacks. Therefore, we argue that all trigger set-based watermarking schemes are vulnerable to this attack scenario; we believe that trigger-based watermarking schemes need another strategy to defend against the ambiguity attack. Representing the learning procedure of our method by encrypted information can be one of them since, without our method, the watermark accuracy of the trigger set shows near zero accuracies, see Table 2.

content.title: Author response
content.comment:
We hope that we could resolve your concerns in the discussion period.

1. Semantic-preserving transformation

We use the ‘semantic-preserving transformation’ term to open the future watermarking way to improve watermarking. The margin-based approach is one of the semantic preserving transformations, so we applied the margin-based approach first in this paper. We hope that the other transformation, such as common corruptions [2,3], can be applied for enhancing the watermarking.

2. Lacks on the previous work of the current work [1]

We would add [1] for our paper. Due to the time limit, we perform the same adversary setup with [1] and borrow the performance of [1] to compare the results. As we can see in Table 5 in [1], the method in [1] shows 0.27 watermark accuracy while ours shows 0.31. We hope that the comparison of the previous work fulfills the reviewer’s concerns.

3. Different attacks

We perform pruning and potential adaptive attacks for our method in Appendix. Here, we also submit the result of fine-tuning, and we hope the result can explain the performance against non-functionality stealing attacks. Additionally, we perform the fine-tuning experiments and our method shows 0.34 watermark accuracy.
Our method is to improve watermarking against black-box attacks, especially functionality stealing attacks since the functionality stealing attack is the most powerful adversary in practice [4]. 

4. Figure 6 is hard to understand

We modify Figure 6 for better understanding.

---
[1] Bansal et al., Certified Neural Network Watermarks with Randomized Smoothing, ICML 2022.

[2] Hendrycks et al., Benchmarking Neural Network Robustness to Common Corruptions and Perturbations, ICLR 2019.

[3] Wong et al., Learning Perturbation Sets for Robust Machine Learning, ICLR 2021.

[4] Lukas et al., SoK: How Robust is Image Classification Deep Neural Network Watermarking?, IEEE S&P 2022.

content.title: Author response
content.comment:
We hope that we could resolve your concerns in the discussion period.

1. The accuracy drop in Table 2 seems big / trials for improving the objective accuracy

As we can see in the results in Table 1, the false mapping for margin-based watermarking does not degrade the objective accuracy while using zero margin, however, it shows the zero watermark accuracy against extraction and distillation. Most of the watermarking methods show low watermark accuracy for watermarked models and near zero accuracy for their extracted counterparts (we can see a similar result in [1]).
We agree that our method shows a trade-off between watermarking and objective accuracy. However, as we can see in Table 2, our method achieves a better sweet-spot than the baseline.
Using randomized noise as a trigger set cannot defend the OOD-filtering adversary, which can reject the ownership verification process from the adversary. The trigger set that we used in our paper guarantees the in-distribution trigger set, which is also empirically proved in Appendix B.5 that our trigger set is not easy to be filtered by the OOD rejection process. Hence, instead of using OOD samples as a trigger set, we demonstrated in Section 4.5 that the owner can choose to improve the objective accuracy by assigning false labels with the highest confidence to the trigger set.

2. The experiments are conducted on the CIFAR10/100 and SVHN.

For computer vision applications, the CIFAR10/100 and SVHN can be considered as small datasets for evaluation. However, we believe that watermarking deep neural networks do not show acceptable performance for CIFAR10/100 and SVHN. In addition, recent studies of watermarking show the performance for CIFAR10/100 and SVHN [2,3].

3. The low accuracy while using the small trigger set

The low accuracy on the trigger set arises from the batching mechanism of our method. Specifically, each training of our method is constructed as follows: the (original) training instance and the trigger instance with a margin contribute the same portion of the training loss, i.e., for $N$ training instance and $M$ trigger instances, the training loss is averaged with $N+M$. This can cause the problem that even with the small size of the trigger set, the trigger sufficiently degrades the objective accuracy since the false mapping can contribute equally to the larger size of the trigger set.
When we use a much bigger size of the trigger set, the false mapping of the trigger set may be effective for degrading the performance. We conduct the experiment on the larger size of the trigger set, and the objective accuracy shows 0.7610, which shows that the number of the trigger set is definitely effective for varying the number of the trigger set. 

4. The motivation for using distillation for evaluating the watermark

The distillation is for evaluating the watermark against the potential adversary which may show better performance than extraction. In the case of trigger-set based watermarking, the trigger-set may have a different mapping of samples with respect to their ground-truth labels. While using the training set of the watermarked model, the surrogate model can diminish the trigger by combining the knowledge from the training set. We introduce the detailed description in Section B.2.

5. Figure 6 is hard to understand

We modify Figure 6 for better understanding.

----
[1] Lukas et al., SoK: How Robust is Image Classification Deep Neural Network Watermarking?, IEEE S&P 2022.

[2] Jia et al., Entangled Watermarks as a defense against model extraction, Usenix Security Symposium 2021.

[3] Bansal et al., Certified Neural Network Watermarks with Randomized Smoothing, ICML 2022.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper proposes an improved method for watermarking neural networks. The authors propose a margin-based approach via input perturbation using the projected gradient ascent method, to improve prior work against functionality-stealing attacks. The authors demonstrated the efficiency of their method on CIFAR10, CIFAR100, and SVHN datasets using ResNet18 and RestNet34.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
**Strengths:**
1) the proposed method is simple and the paper is easy to follow.
2) results suggest the proposed method is better than the evaluated baselines, considering several functionality-stealing methods.
3) the authors provide an ablation study to analyze each of the components involved with the proposed method.

**Weaknesses:**
1) results are reported on a somewhat artificial setup (CIFAR10/100 and SVHN) using ResNet models only. additionally, the results are reported only for image classification. 
2) some of the results and analysis are not clear (see detailed comments below).
3) the proposed method is mainly a mix of two methods (trigger-based watermarking where we generate the trigger-set using PGA). This by itself does not necessarily a bad thing, however, the evaluation setup is limited.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
**Clarity:** The paper is clearly written.

**Novelty:** The novelty of the proposed approach is limited (see more details above and below).

**Reproducibility:** The authors provide the source code to reproduce the results.
content.summary_of_the_review:
Overall, the paper is clearly written and the method is well-motivated. As I stated above, the method is simple and a combination of two well-known methods. This by itself is not a bad thing, however, the evaluation is pretty limited to toyish image classification models, in this case, it is not clear whether this method can generalize to other domains/tasks/models/etc.

**Comments and questions:**
1) In Table 2, we see a big drop in performance when embedding the trigger set, for instance from ~60% accuracy without a watermark to ~50% with a watermark. The authors discussed it a bit in the results section, however, prior work did not suffer that much from such performance degradation (for instance [1]). The authors point out the trade-off between accuracy and resistance to the watermarked results, so my question is, did the authors try to use a different trigger set? maybe random noise? 

2) In Figure 3, it seems like using a smaller number of images in the trigger set hurts the model performance compared to a bigger trigger set (Figure 3a). This is counter-intuitive to me, as I expect more "noisy samples" would hurt model performance and not the other way around.

3) Figure 6: it is very hard to recognize the shapes of the dots, can the authors please make them bigger? In the beginning, I did not even realize there is a difference between them. 

4) Can the authors please explain the motivation for using distillation as in 4.1? If the adversary has access to the training data and labels used to train the watermarked model, can't he just learn it independently from the watermarked model? 

[1] Adi, Yossi, et al. "Turning your weakness into a strength: Watermarking deep neural networks by backdooring." 27th USENIX Security Symposium (USENIX Security 18). 2018.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper proposes a method for improving the watermarking of deep neural networks through adversarial training. The method maximizes the margin of neighboring models with differing  predictions on the trigger set. Empirically, the method improves the performance on distillation attacks.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths: 
* The problem of watermarking neural networks resistant to attacks is significant. 
* Empirically, the method proves to be robust against distillation attacks. 


Weakness:
1. The writing of the paper could be improved. There are several grammatical errors and also the writing of the paper makes it hard to follow key results. For example, Equation 2 mentions a "semantic-preserving transformation", but the definition of which is nowhere to be found later and does not seem to be relevant to the main algorithm. 

2. Comparison with existing work (defense) is lacking: 
Only one method is used as comparison. More recent work in this area should be referenced and compared to. 
Arpit Bansal, Ping-yeh Chiang, Michael J Curry, Rajiv Jain, Curtis Wigington, Varun Manjunatha,
John P Dickerson, and Tom Goldstein. Certified neural network watermarks with randomized
smoothing. 

3. Methods of attacks is also lacking. 
There are many more black-box attacks in addition to the definition of distillation used in the paper.  The authors could consider adding more benchmarks for attacks. 
- Finetuning.
- Pruning. 

4. Fig 3 (a)'s results are surprising and hard to interpret.
Why would objective accuracy increase when the size of the trigger set is increased?  Conceptually a trigger set has the wrong labels so fitting on a larger trigger set would be detrimental to the accuracy on benign data.   Moreover, from Figure 3, it seems that a trigger set size of (40 - 80) is optimal. Why is trigger-set=100 selected? 
Also # queries and trigger set size is used interchangeably without notice.

Quality:  See Weakness.
Novelty: Good.
Reproducibility: Good.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper proposes a margin-based DNN watermarking approach to improve the model’s robustness against functionality stealing attacks (in particular, distillation and extraction). The approach is similar to adversarial training in that the DNN’s training loss composes the loss for the training set as well as the loss for the adversarial attacked trigger set. The intuition is that the margins of the trigger set samples increase and thus the trigger set samples are less likely to be inferred correctly by the attacker’s distilled / extracted models.For evaluation, the author compares the proposed approach against one baseline under different attack settings on three vision datasets.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
## Pros

-intuitive approach and the writing is easy to follow

-the improved robustness is promising

-experimental analysis of the proposed approach is well conducted 

## Cons

-the proposed approach is incremental in the sense it is basically adversarial training but limits the adversarial loss to only the trigger set.

-the experiments are all conducted only on small datasets (e.g., CIFAR-10) for which the model can be trained very fast and invalidates the motivation on functionality stealing attack.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
## Clarity

The paper is well-written and very clear.

## Quality

The claims are mostly well supported. One issue is as I mentioned earlier, the small datasets experiments make the motivation on improving the watermarking robustness much weaker since the attacker can simply train such a small model on a small dataset on their own.

## Novelty

As I said earlier, the technical novelty is only incremental. It has some experimental novelty since the approach has not been used before for watermarking robustness. However, this task is still similar to adversarial robustness and in the vision domain so the novelty is also limited from this perspective.

## Reproducibility

Code is provided and the method is easy to understand so it is likely to be reproduced.

content.title: Margin-based Neural Network Watermarking
content.TL;DR: We propose margin-based watermarking for deep neural networks.
content.abstract: As Machine Learning as a Service (MLaaS) platforms become prevalent, deep neural network (DNN) watermarking has gained increasing attention, which enables one to verify the ownership of a target DNN model in a black-box scenario. Unfortunately, previous watermarking methods are vulnerable to functionality stealing attacks, thus allowing an adversary to falsely claim the ownership of a DNN model stolen from its original owner. In this work, we propose a novel margin-based DNN watermarking approach that is robust to the functionality stealing attacks based on model extraction and distillation. Specifically, during training, our method maximizes the margins of watermarked samples by using projected gradient ascent on them so that their predicted labels cannot change without compromising the accuracy of the model that the attacker tries to steal. We validate our method on multiple benchmarks and show that our watermarking method successfully defends against model extraction attacks, outperforming recent baselines.
